headline: The biggest adjustment is that Qatar's public and business life runs on stricter modesty, punctuality and gender-aware greeting rules than the relaxed, harmony-first style you know from the Philippines.

watch_outs.title: Wait for a handshake cue
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines you greet with a smile and handshake, and a light cheek-to-cheek greeting is common with friends and family.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Qatar some people, especially women, prefer not to shake hands with the opposite sex and may place a hand on the heart instead.
watch_outs.do: Offer a smile and a verbal greeting, and extend your hand only if the other person offers theirs first.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not reach out to shake a Qatari woman's hand unless she extends hers first.

watch_outs.title: Dress modestly in public
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines shorts and sleeveless tops are everyday wear, with modest dress mainly expected in churches and rural areas.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Qatar shoulders and knees should be covered in public, and shorts, skirts and sleeveless tops are prohibited in government buildings and mosques, where women must also cover their hair.
watch_outs.do: Pack loose clothing that covers shoulders and knees, and carry a scarf for mosque visits.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not wear shorts or sleeveless tops to government offices or mosques.

watch_outs.title: Greet elders and women first
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines younger people address elders with titles and respect, but greeting order is usually casual and flexible.
watch_outs.to_norm: When entering a Qatari home, greet people by status and age, with the elderly and those of higher status first, and also greet the women.
watch_outs.do: On entering a home, greet the oldest and most senior people first, then the women, before settling in.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not walk in and greet only the person you know best.

watch_outs.title: Keep public affection restrained
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines brief hand-holding is fine and kissing or long embraces are saved for private settings, especially around elders.
watch_outs.to_norm: Qatar is more conservative in public, so keep physical affection between couples minimal in malls, streets and family gatherings.
watch_outs.do: Limit affection to brief hand-holding and save embraces for private settings.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not kiss or embrace your partner in public places.

watch_outs.title: Don't offer your left hand
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines eating with a fork and spoon in either hand is completely normal and goes unnoticed.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Qatar the right hand is used for eating, greeting and giving or receiving items, and the left hand is considered unclean.
watch_outs.do: Use your right hand for food, handshakes and passing dishes or gifts.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not eat, greet or hand over items with your left hand.

watch_outs.title: Leave a little food when full
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines you hesitate and then accept at least a small portion when a host offers food, and clearing your plate is normal.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Qatar a host may press you to eat more, and leaving a tiny portion of food signals that you are full and the host was generous.
watch_outs.do: Accept the food offered, and when full leave a small amount on the plate rather than refusing outright.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not refuse food outright or scrape your plate completely clean if you want to signal you are full.

watch_outs.title: Arrive on time for work
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines relaxed 'Filipino time' is fine socially, though business meetings call for arriving on time.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Qatar business meetings and official appointments expect punctuality, and arriving late reads as disrespectful.
watch_outs.do: Arrive on time or a few minutes early for meetings and work commitments.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not treat Qatari business appointments with the relaxed timing you might use for a social gathering.

watch_outs.title: Keep feet off furniture and away from people
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines showing the soles of your feet is a minor faux pas, mainly avoided by not propping feet on furniture at someone's home.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Qatar showing the soles of your feet toward others, or placing feet toward people, is considered disrespectful during meals and visits.
watch_outs.do: Keep both feet flat on the floor and pointed away from others when sitting.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not cross your ankle over your knee so a sole faces someone, or put your feet on a table.

watch_outs.title: Tip where service charge is absent
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines tipping is appreciated but not mandatory, and you check the bill for a service charge before leaving about 10% in cash.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Qatar tipping is not always expected, but in restaurants a tip of around 10% is welcome when no service charge is already added.
watch_outs.do: Check the bill for a service charge and, if none is included, leave a modest cash tip.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not assume a tip is required or leave one on top of an included service charge.

watch_outs.title: Bring a modest gift to a home
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines a modest, well-wrapped gift such as sweets or fruit is welcome when invited to a home, and it may not be opened right away.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Qatar bringing something small such as dates or sweets when invited to a home is a nice gesture, and gifts may also not be opened immediately.
watch_outs.do: Bring a modest gift such as dates or sweets, and offer it with your right hand.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not bring alcohol or anything containing pork as a gift.
